Linda Woo is a 58-year-old cisgender woman of Chinese Asian descent who uses she/her pronouns and lives in Richmond, on the traditional territories of the Musqueam, Tsawwassen, Squamish, and Tsleil-Waututh peoples. She has three grown children and two grandchildren. Her husband died 10 years before February 20, 2023, and she has a new male friend. Her occupation was not discussed.

In a medical-student case scenario, the user is a second-year medical student working in gynecologist Dr. Sandman’s office in Richmond. Linda Woo, described as healthy-looking and 58 years old, was referred by her family physician for assessment and management of abnormal vaginal bleeding. She had a three-month history of occasional pinkish vaginal discharge noticed when wiping after using the bathroom and seen a couple of times on her underwear. Her family physician performed a Pap smear two months before the February 20, 2023 case discussion, when Linda presented with vaginal bleeding; the smear was reported as moderate squamous dyskaryosis.

Linda Woo’s Pap smear was described as showing combined moderate dyskaryosis and HPV changes, with both LSIL and HSIL features. On the right side, two superficial intermediate squamous cells with koilocytotic changes and dyskaryotic nuclei, plus a dyskeratotic cell described as a “button,” suggest CIN 1 and HPV infection (LSIL). In the center-left field, dyskaryotic, overlapped, and stripped deep intermediate nuclei indicate at least CIN 2 (HSIL); this worst area accounts for the HSIL-with-HPV-changes report. Histology showed areas of CIN 1, CIN 2, and CIN 3.

On 2023-02-20, the assistant explained that CIN means cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, abnormal cell growth on the cervical surface, often detected through cervical screening. CIN 1 is mild, CIN 2 moderate, and CIN 3 severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ; the assistant said Mrs. Woo’s Pap smear showed areas of CIN 1, 2, and 3.

For a case discussion about Mrs. Woo, the assistant suggested asking about menstrual changes, sexual and obstetric history, prior abnormal Pap tests or cervical dysplasia/cancer, family history of cervical, vulvar, or endometrial cancer, relevant medical conditions or bleeding disorders, genital pain/itching/discharge, rectal bleeding, urinary symptoms, and abdominal pain. Suggested focused examination steps were external genital inspection, speculum examination of the vagina and cervix, bimanual examination of the uterus and ovaries, and rectal examination.
records.topic: Differential diagnosis and examination for bleeding

records.text: The assistant described Pap smear collection as using a speculum to visualize the cervix, then a spatula and/or brush to collect cervical cells, particularly from the transformation zone where ectocervical squamous cells meet endocervical glandular cells. It said the sampling location generally does not change over a woman's life, though technique may vary. It identified early detection of cellular changes, relative affordability, ease of administration, and office-based, non-invasive collection as screening advantages. The assistant stated that British Columbia screening guidelines recommend screening women aged 25–69 and that women under 25 generally do not need screening unless abnormal results or other risk factors are present.

The assistant defined dyskaryosis as abnormal or atypical cellular changes, dysplasia as abnormal cell growth or development that can be precancerous, and neoplasia as abnormal cell growth that may be benign or malignant. It said Mrs. Woo’s reported moderate squamous dyskaryosis with HPV changes indicates abnormal cervical cells that may progress to cancer. It distinguished premalignant lesions, which show dysplasia without invasion, from malignant lesions, in which cancerous cells invade surrounding tissues and may spread.
